answer.rationale: The strongest signal is temporal: a release landed 2 hours ago and write-path p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, which fits a release-induced regression better than the alternatives. Failover (b2) moves traffic but carries write-loss and split-brain risk at settlement peak and does nothing if the bad code ships in every region. Capacity (b3) and read-replica routing (b5) address load-shaped problems; settlement peak is expected load, and neither undoes a regression. A circuit breaker (b4) helps when a downstream dependency fails fast, but there is no partner-outage signal here. So rollback is the intervention most likely to remove the cause rather than mask it. I spend the single verification on memory_b1 because it is the memory my plan leans on hardest and it is the one most likely to be over-generalized: the consolidated summary says rollback 'cleared the checkout error spike,' which is an error-rate symptom, not a climbing write-latency curve, and it asserts 'the prior build was stable' and 'no customer impact' without saying whether that rollback happened under heavy write load or whether it involved schema/data migrations. If the archived record shows day-18 was a low-traffic, migration-free rollback, its transfer to a settlement-peak write-heavy window is much weaker and I would tighten the guard or reconsider. Downstream risk: rolling back during peak writes can strand in-flight writes and, if the release included a forward-only migration, a rollback could corrupt or drop settlement records — that is a customer-write loss, which the primary objective forbids, so the abort condition is any evidence of non-reversible migration. Scale is deliberately small and guarded rather than fleet-wide: revert on a single write shard or canary cohort first (b6 shows canary cohorts surface regressions within an hour, and the same gate works in reverse to confirm a fix), watch p99 and write-success on that slice, and only widen in the next window if latency responds. This keeps the one-intervention budget from becoming an irreversible fleet-wide bet on a memory whose original context I have not yet read. I am not certain the release is causal; concurrent settlement peak could mean genuine saturation, in which case rollback will show no improvement on the guarded slice and capacity becomes the next-window candidate.
